pageTitle: Bloom filters, explained with a guest list
title: The doorman who only remembers hints
subtitle: A hands-on tour of Bloom filters, in six short steps.

paras: Say you run a mail server and you keep a list of known spam addresses. Millions of them. Every incoming message needs one question answered fast: is this sender on the list? Storing the whole list in memory on every server is expensive, and checking it on disk is slow.

Here's the trick: you don't need the list. You need something that says "definitely not on it" most of the time, so you can skip the expensive check, and "maybe on it" the rest of the time, when you go and look properly.

Picture a doorman with a terrible memory who instead remembers three hints about every guest: hat, accent, shoe colour. A stranger with the same hat, accent and shoes gets waved through. Anyone missing a hint is turned away with total confidence. That doorman is a Bloom filter.

The doorman's memory is a row of switches, all off at the start. To add a guest, scramble their name three different ways; each scramble picks one switch, and you flip it on. To check a name, scramble it the same three ways and look: if any switch is off, that name was never added.
Add a few names and watch switches flip. Then check a name you never added and see the doorman reject it on the spot.

Here's the catch. Switches never turn off, and different names can share switches. Fill the row with enough guests and a stranger's three switches will all happen to be on. The doorman says "maybe" about someone who was never invited. That's a false positive, and it's the price of the memory savings.
Play with the row length and the number of scrambles per name. Longer rows and more scrambles push false positives down, until the row gets crowded and they climb again.

origin.intro: In 1970, Burton H. Bloom, working at Computer Usage Company in Massachusetts, published a short paper in Communications of the ACM called "Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors". The whole idea fits in a few pages.

timeline.label: The problem
timeline.text: Memory was tiny and disks were slow. Bloom's example was a program that hyphenates English words: about 90% follow simple rules, but the rest, around 50,000 words, need a dictionary that only fits on disk.

timeline.label: The naive fix
timeline.text: Look every word up on disk, or try to squeeze a full hash table of the exceptions into memory. The first is slow; the second doesn't fit.

timeline.label: The insight
timeline.text: Store a blurry version of the exception list in memory and accept a small rate of wrong answers. Bloom showed that allowing a few false positives cut disk lookups by roughly 84% in his example.

timeline.label: Since then
timeline.text: The idea stayed a niche database trick for decades, then spread through networking and web systems in the late 1990s and 2000s. Relatives followed: counting Bloom filters that can delete, and cuckoo filters that pack tighter.

origin.takeaway: Bloom traded a little correctness for a lot of memory. Every use since has been a version of that same trade.

uses.intro: Anywhere a fast "definitely not" lets a system skip expensive work.

items.title: Databases with many files on disk
items.text: Apache Cassandra keeps a Bloom filter per data file so a lookup can skip files that definitely don't hold the key. RocksDB and LevelDB-style stores do the same.

items.title: Web browsers and URL blocklists
items.text: Early versions of Google Chrome used a Bloom filter to check URLs against its Safe Browsing list before asking the server.

items.title: Content delivery networks
items.text: Akamai uses Bloom filters to avoid caching objects that are requested only once, so one-hit wonders don't fill the cache.

uses.caveat: What it can't do: it never says a definite "yes", so you still need the real list for the maybes, and a standard Bloom filter can't remove an item, because switching a bit off could erase someone else's hint.

claims.text: Burton H. Bloom published the Bloom filter in 1970.
Bloom worked at Computer Usage Company in Massachusetts.
The paper appeared in Communications of the ACM.
The paper is titled Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors.
Bloom's motivating example was a hyphenation program for English words.
In Bloom's example about 90% of words could be hyphenated by simple rules.
In Bloom's example around 50,000 words needed a dictionary lookup.
Allowing false positives cut disk lookups by roughly 84% in Bloom's example.
Bloom filters became widely used in networking and web systems in the late 1990s and 2000s.
Cuckoo filters are a later alternative that uses less space.
Apache Cassandra keeps a Bloom filter per SSTable to skip files that do not contain a key.
RocksDB and LevelDB-style stores use Bloom filters per file.
Early versions of Google Chrome used a Bloom filter for Safe Browsing URL checks.
Akamai uses Bloom filters to avoid caching one-hit wonders.
A standard Bloom filter cannot delete an item.
